state.misconception_label: Thinks you can find missing values in a given table by treating the row as linear and adding on the difference between the first two values given.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The equation \( f=3 r^{2}+3 \) is used to find values in the table below. What is the value covered by the star? \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline\( r \) & \( 1 \) & \( 2 \) & \( 3 \) & \( 4 \) \\ \hline\( f \) & \( 6 \) & \( 15 \) & \( \color{gold}\bigstar \) & \\ \hline \end{tabular}. I got \( 24 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Why do you think adding on the difference between the first two values is the right approach to find the missing value in the table? Can you explain your reasoning behind this method?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Well, I thought that since the numbers in the table go up in a pattern, I could just keep adding the same amount each time... so I added 9 (the difference between 6 and 15) to 15 to get 24. But now I'm wondering if that only works for some tables and not others? Should I be using the equation instead?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Why do you think the pattern of adding the same amount each time only works for some tables and not others? Can you think of a specific reason why that method might not be reliable for all situations?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, I think it's because... like, if the equation has something squared in it, then maybe the differences between the numbers get bigger each time? So adding the same amount wouldn't work because the pattern isn't actually linear? But I'm still not really sure how to tell when to use the equation versus just looking at the pattern...

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively engages the specific linear-pattern misconception through questioning that prompts the student to discover why constant differences fail for quadratic relationships, leading to visible improvement in the student's understanding by Turn 4, though the teacher could have provided more concrete guidance on when to use the equation.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking, never provides the answer directly, and implicitly helps the student discover the flaw in assuming constant differences work for all patterns, which is a textbook example of Socratic teaching.
